summary: profitability index (PI) is what the Profitability index calculator works out, and it gets there from the initial investment, the PV of future cash flow and the discount rate. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Profitability index calculator work?
sections.html:
The Profitability index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports profitability index (PI) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the initial investment, the PV of future cash flow, the initial investment (Future cash flows) and the discount rate.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Profitability index calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Profitability index (PI)=PV of future cash flow ÷ initial investment
Total PV of future cash flows=((year 1 ÷ (discount rate + 1)) + (year 10 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 10)) + (year 2 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 2)) + (year 3 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 3)) + (year 4 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 4)) + (year 5 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 5)) + (year 6 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 6)) + (year 7 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 7)) + (year 8 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 8)) + (year 9 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 9)))
Profitability index=(((year 1 ÷ (discount rate + 1)) + (year 10 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 10)) + (year 2 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 2)) + (year 3 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 3)) + (year 4 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 4)) + (year 5 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 5)) + (year 6 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 6)) + (year 7 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 7)) + (year 8 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 8)) + (year 9 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 9))) ÷ initial investment)
PV for year 1=(year 1 ÷ (discount rate + 1))
PV for year 2=(year 2 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 2))
PV for year 3=(year 3 ÷ (discount rate + 1 ^ 3))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Initial investment = 10, Discount rate = 10 %, Number of years = 30 and Year 1 = 10. Working through the relationship above gives PV for year 1 = 9, PV for year = 8, PV for year = 8 and PV for year 4 = 7.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: PV for year 1 = 9, PV for year = 8, PV for year = 8 and PV for year 4 = 7 should be roughly the size you expected from Initial investment = 10 and Discount rate = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Profitability index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the initial investment, the PV of future cash flow and the discount rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Profitability index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns profitability index (PI), derived from the initial investment, the PV of future cash flow and the discount rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Profitability index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial investment, the PV of future cash flow and the discount rate, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial investment in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial investment opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports PV for year 1 = 9. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Profitability index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
